query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Inducing nanoscale short‐range ordering of chromium (and associated elements) in corrosion‐resistant steels promotes the formation of a denser, more adherent passive oxide layer, thereby enhancing their resistance to chemical attack.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional alloy or stainless steel with a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements (e.g., chromium, molybdenum) as typically found in steels for chemical-processing or nuclear-power applications.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored heat-treatment (annealing) designed to induce short-range ordering and nanocluster formation of Cr-rich regions, versus a standard homogenization treatment.
generation.conditions: Corrosion tests conducted in simulated operational environments (e.g., elevated temperature, moderate pressure, aqueous saline or coolant chemistry representative of chemical-processing or nuclear-power systems) in a controlled laboratory setting.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale Cr-rich clusters and localized chemical ordering within the steel microstructure that serve as templates for the nucleation and growth of a protective chromium oxide passive film.
generation.mechanism: The engineered short-range ordering causes chromium (and possibly molybdenum) to segregate into nanoclusters which, upon exposure to an oxidizing environment, locally promote the rapid formation of a uniform and compact passive film. This film acts as a barrier to corrosive species, reducing ion diffusion and limiting material degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel samples treated to induce short-range ordering will develop a more uniform and robust passive oxide layer, resulting in lower corrosion current densities and reduced material loss compared to baseline homogenized samples under identical corrosive testing conditions.
generation.baseline: Steels with identical bulk composition that have been subjected only to standard homogenization heat treatments without promoting nanocluster formation, which are expected to form a less compact or uniform passive film and exhibit higher corrosion rates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in steels with sufficient chromium content (e.g., >10–20 wt% Cr) and under environmental conditions typical for chemical processing and nuclear power (moderate to high temperature aqueous environments). Its applicability might be limited if the heat-treatment regime or alloy composition does not support detectable short-range ordering.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contribution of short-range ordering relative to other microstructural factors (such as grain size, residual stresses, or secondary phases) in governing corrosion protection remains to be fully determined. In addition, variations in ordering kinetics between different steel grades may introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical steel samples with high chromium content: one set receiving a controlled heat-treatment designed to induce short-range ordering (and Cr-rich nanoclusters) and a control set receiving a homogenization treatment that minimizes ordering. Subject both sets to identical, standardized corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization tests in a 3.5% NaCl solution at elevated temperature).
measurements: Corrosion current density (i_corr) from polarization curves
Characterization of the passive film using surface analysis (e.g., XPS, SEM-EDS)
Microstructural analysis (TEM/SEM) to confirm the presence and extent of Cr-rich nanoclusters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (i.e., lower i_corr, more uniform and thicker passive film) compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis that induced short-range ordering enhances corrosion resistance is falsified.

Microstructure, Thermal, and Corrosion Behavior of the AlAgCuNiSnTi Equiatomic Multicomponent Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe paper presents the microstructure and corrosion behavior of an AlTiNiCuAgSn new equiatomic multicomponent alloy. The alloy was obtained using the vacuum arc remelting (VAR) technique in MRF-ABJ900 equipment. The microstructural analysis was performed by optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM microscope, SEM-EDS) and the phase transformations were highlighted by dilatometric analysis and differential thermal analysis (DTA). The results show that the as-cast alloy microstructure is three-phase, with an average microhardness of 487 HV0.1/15. The obtained alloy could be included in the group of compositionally complex alloys (CCA). The corrosion resistance was studied using the potentiodynamic method in saline solution with 3.5% NaCl. Considering the high corrosion resistance, the obtained alloy can be used for surface coating applications.Keywords: high entropy alloy, equiatomic multicomponent alloy, microstructure, corrosion resistance, surface coatings

Erosion and Corrosion Resistance Performance of Laser Metal Deposited High-Entropy Alloy Coatings at Hellisheidi Geothermal Site

Abstract: AbstractGeothermal process equipment and accessories are usually manufactured from low-alloy steels which offer affordability but increase the susceptibility of the materials to corrosion. Applying erosion-corrosion-resistant coatings to these components could represent an economical solution to the problem. In this work, testing of two newly developed laser metal deposited high-entropy alloy (LMD-HEA) coatings—CoCrFeNiMo0.85 and Al0.5CoCrFeNi, applied to carbon and stainless steels—was carried out at the Hellisheidi geothermal power plant. Tests in three different geothermal environments were performed at the Hellisheidi site: wellhead test at 194 °C and 14 bar, erosion test at 198 °C and 15 bar, and aerated test at 90 °C and 1 bar. Data-driven electron-diffraction approach reveals local short-range ordering in CrCoNi with ordering effects

Abstract: The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys
